title: How long to keep homeschool records
dek: Separate required records, lasting academic evidence, and ordinary work samples. Verify local retention rules before clearing a school-year box.
metaDescription: Separate required records, lasting academic evidence, and ordinary work samples. Verify local retention rules before clearing a school-year box.

paragraphs: Keep homeschool records for at least the period required by the rules governing your program. Separately, retain lasting academic evidence such as a final high-school transcript and the records supporting it. There is no universal two- or three-year rule that tells every US homeschool family when it is safe to discard everything.

A school-year box often contains three different collections: evidence you must keep, evidence you may need later, and things you love. Sorting those purposes before deciding dates prevents a large pile from hiding the one report you actually need.

body.heading: Make three retention groups
rows: Attendance, portfolios, evaluations, notices, filing receipts
Follow the applicable rules; confirm the relevant period and accepted format.
Final transcript, course descriptions, credit calculations, graduation record
Retain long term as a practical recommendation, with reliable backups.
Duplicate practice sheets, project photos, first stories
Select after checking legal and future-use needs; separate memories from compliance.

body.heading: Use a state example without turning it into a national deadline
paragraphs: [Florida's home education statute](https://wwwo.leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=1000-1099%2F1002%2FSections%2F1002.41.html%2F) requires the portfolio under that provision to be preserved for two years. Its contents include an activity log made contemporaneously with instruction, reading titles, and work samples. That is a specific legal example, not a disposal instruction for every kind of record or program.

Read your current statute and education department guidance, checking the schooling route as well as the state. If the start of a retention period or the sufficiency of electronic copies is unclear, obtain a specific answer before shredding originals. Keep the answer with your retention note.

body.heading: Review a year before discarding anything
items: Identify the child, school year, and governing homeschool program.
List the records that were required and confirm their retention rule.
Check for pending evaluations, official requests, transfers, or disputes.
Select academic evidence that may support future transcripts or applications.
Separate sentimental material so it is not mistaken for required evidence.
Check scans for complete pages, legible dates, and readable annotations.
Open the backup from a second location before disposing of originals.
Record what you discarded and the reason for the decision.

body.heading: Invented example: one third-grade box
paragraphs: A parent finds 40 arithmetic worksheets, a reading list, an evaluation, filing correspondence, and a large model bridge. The family first checks which documents its program requires. It keeps the required set and filing proof intact, selects dated samples where permitted, and photographs the bridge with a note explaining the assignment.

The photograph makes the project easier to store, but it does not automatically replace an original that a rule requires. Likewise, an unused teacher manual may be reusable, while a completed workbook or a list of reading titles may be evidence. 'Curriculum' is not a single disposal category.

body.heading: High school needs a different level of care
paragraphs: A final transcript is easier to support if you retain the underlying course names, dates, credit decisions, grading methods, and relevant assessments. Keep final records in an openable format, with a private backup and a trusted person's knowledge of where they are stored. This is a practical preservation recommendation, not a claim that every document has a permanent legal retention requirement.

Before graduation or a move, check what the intended college, employer, licensing body, or receiving school actually requests. Do not assume every institution wants the same documents. Preserve relevant originals until you have resolved the specific need.

body.heading: An app is not automatically an archive
paragraphs: Know whether your tool limits visible history, exported entries, attachments, or access after account closure. Export before a limit could omit older work. Use a filename such as 'Child-school-year-export-date,' then check the earliest and latest entries and any attachment links.

A useful review point is term end and before changing tools, with an additional export whenever your tool's limits require it. Keep an independent copy. A PDF that points to photos in a closed account is not a complete archive of those photos.

items.line: For [program and school year], which records must be retained, for how long, and may a legible electronic copy replace the original?
Does this export contain the complete record for [child and period], including older entries and attachments, or is any history excluded?

body.heading: When to pause disposal
paragraphs: Stop if there is an unresolved official request, appeal, legal dispute, or uncertainty about a required document. Seek qualified local advice where necessary. Do not use an ordinary decluttering schedule to destroy potentially relevant evidence.

For keeping new records manageable without deciding their final lifespan every day, use [the simple record keeping system](/guides/simple-homeschool-record-keeping-system). Retention decisions belong in a periodic review, not in the middle of teaching.

items.q: Can I throw away completed workbooks?
items.a: Sometimes, after preserving any required materials and useful academic evidence. Check the governing rules first. Keep enough context to identify the child, date, subject, and purpose of retained samples; a handful of anonymous pages may not serve the same job as the original book.

items.q: Do I need to keep everything forever?
items.a: No universal rule requires that. Separate legal requirements from your own long-term preservation choices. Final academic records and filing evidence often deserve more care than repeated practice sheets, but pending requests or disputes can change an otherwise ordinary disposal decision.

Only when the copy serves the needed purpose and your applicable rules accept it. Check readability, completeness, dates, and backup access before discarding originals. Keep attachments independently when an export only links to them, and preserve originals while a specific acceptance question remains unresolved.

sources.name: Florida Legislature: section 1002.41
sources.note: Florida home education portfolio provisions require two-year preservation and include a contemporaneous activity log, reading titles, and work samples; this applies to the specified program, not nationwide.
